paper_title: Inhabitant: An Agent Framework for Long-Horizon Human-Scene Interaction with Spatial Control and Quantitative Feedback

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Recent work on human-scene interaction (HSI) generation moves from single interactions to long-horizon interaction, where a language-model agent plans and executes a sequence of interactions in a 3D scene under one instruction. However, existing agents struggle in challenging everyday scenarios (e.g., picking up a toy and throwing it into a basket) because they lack spatial control over the motion and quantitative feedback on its execution, and they often fail to complete the interaction sequence. To address these gaps, we present Inhabitant, a training-free agent framework in which the agent specifies each motion through positions, paths and poses, measures how the executed interaction deviates from its intent, and revises the control specification accordingly. For an extensive evaluation in such scenarios, we build Inhabit, a benchmark of 75 household tasks in 31 furniture layouts of an apartment, in which every task chains one to three goals on movable objects and is carried out by the whole body, excluding fingers. On Inhabit, Inhabitant completes 98.7\% of the tasks with Claude Opus 5.5, and 93.3\% and 82.7\% with Claude Sonnet 5.5 and Gemini 4 Argon, respectively. Ablations confirm that without spatial control the agent fails most tasks, and without quantitative feedback its motion becomes less precise. Code is available on the project page.

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Recent work on human-scene interaction (HSI) generation moves from single interactions to long-horizon interaction, where language-model agent plans and executes sequence of interactions in 3D scene under one instruction. However, existing agents struggle in challenging everyday scenarios (e.g., picking up toy and throwing it into basket) because they lack spatial control over the motion and quantitative feedback on its execution, and they often fail to complete the interaction sequence. To address these gaps, we present Inhabitant, training-free agent framework in which the agent specifies each motion through positions, paths and poses, measures how the executed interaction deviates from its intent, and revises the control specification accordingly. For an extensive evaluation in such scenarios, we build Inhabit, benchmark of 75 household tasks in 31 furniture layouts of an apartment, in which every task chains one to three goals on movable objects and is carried out by the whole body, excluding fingers. On Inhabit, Inhabitant completes 98.7% of the tasks with Claude Opus 5.5, and 93.3% and 82.7% with Claude Sonnet 5.5 and Gemini 4 Argon, respectively. Ablations confirm that without spatial control the agent fails most tasks, and without quantitative feedback its motion becomes less precise. Code, the benchmark and video are available on the project page. 1. Introduction Human-scene interaction (HSI) generation, which synthesizes how person moves through scene and acts on its objects, is core problem for computer graphics and embodied AI [7, 8, 29, 38]. Early work typically focuses on isolated, short-horizon interactions: single action involving one target object, such as sitting down on chair, standing up from chair, or picking up an object [14, 18, 25, 47, 61, 64]. Recent work has shifted towards more challenging setting of long-horizon interaction, where language-model agent plans and executes sequence of interactions in 3D scene under one instruction, for example, put the cube in the basket, kick the ball under the table and put the cushion back on the sofa. These scenes are often simulated environments that respond physically to the body [1, 12, 37, 43, 51, 52, 60]. However, existing agents often fail to complete such sequence when every interaction must be executed through full-body motion (Fig. 1a). In the example above, the agent first tries to pick up the cube, but the hand does not reach close enough to grasp it and closes few centimetres away. The agent cannot correct this failure: text prompt cannot specify the required hand position precisely, and rendered frames do not quantify the spatial error. We investigate such failures by adapting three representative agents to these scenarios (Sec. 5.2) and attribute them to two causes, both concerning the interface between the agent and the generated interaction. First, the control is mostly high-level: the agent conditions the human motion only on skill with one parameter [37], text description of each step [49, 60], or few contact or goal positions [12, 52]. As result, it cannot specify the motion at the level of precise positions, paths and poses. Second, the feedback is absent or qualitative: most agents plan the interaction once and never observe its outcome [43, 51, 52], including the few that write poses for motion generator [1, 30]. Other agents observe only rendered frames [37, 60], which may show that an interaction failed but cannot indicate precisely how far the executed interaction deviates from its intent. We present Inhabitant, training-free agent framework that turns long-horizon human-scene interaction into closed-loop spatial control problem (Fig. 1b). The key novelty is to expose two interfaces that existing agents lack: spatially grounded control over generated whole-body motion and quantitative feedback on its physical execution. For control, the agent directly writes the control specification of pretrained motion generator, Kimodo [32], and specifies the motion by positions, paths and poses rather than only high-level skills or text prompts. For feedback, each motion 1 Figure 1. One step of household task: picking up cube from the counter. (a) Existing agents control the motion through text prompt or skill and receive no feedback or only rendered frames; after the hand misses the cube, the agent can only reword the prompt, and the hand misses again. (b) Inhabitant measures how far the hand stopped from the cube (quantitative feedback), fixes where the right hand must be at given frame (spatial control), and grasps the cube on the next try. The frames in (a) come from our agent restricted to text prompts. is executed in scene simulator with half-physics [36]; the agent then queries measurements of the body and the scene, such as positions, distances and contacts, to quantify how the executed interaction deviates from its intent. It revises the control specification using the measured deviation. The two interfaces close loop: the agent proposes motion, executes it, measures the outcome, revises the specification and commits the result as short motion segment only when the measurements match its intent. By composing such verified segments, Inhabitant builds complete interaction sequence segment by segment. For an extensive evaluation in such challenging everyday scenarios, we build Inhabit  (Fig. 3)  , new benchmark of 75 household tasks in 31 furniture layouts of the ReplicaCAD apartment [39, 56], simulated with half-physics [36] in line with HumanCLAW [37]. Each task states one to three goals, such as placing an object, throwing it or moving it with foot; ten tasks additionally combine goal with body posture, such as sitting, lying or kneeling. The goals are designed to require coordinated use of the hands, the feet and whole-body posture. Inhabit differs from previous benchmarks in two respects. First, HSI benchmarks typically evaluate single interaction with static target at time, such as walking to piece of furniture and sitting on it [37, 47]. In contrast, Inhabit chains multiple interactions with movable objects under single instruction, so the outcome of one interaction, including its errors, becomes the initial condition for the next. Second, embodied household benchmarks also contain long-horizon tasks, but agents usually solve them by calling predefined skills such as navigating, picking and placing [3, 56]. In Inhabit, every step must instead be realized through generated whole-body motion, excluding fingers, so the benchmark tests whether the body can reach, hold and move an object through physically executed motion. success rule judges the physical outcome, while collisions, disturbed objects and foot skate measure the quality of the motion. On Inhabit, Inhabitant completes 74 of the 75 tasks (98.7%) with Claude Opus 5.5 as the agent, and 93.3% and 82.7% of them with Claude Sonnet 5.5 and Gemini 4 Argon, respectively. By comparison, the best of three existing agents adapted to Inhabit completes only 26.7% with Claude Opus 5.5. Ablations show that without spatial control the agent fails most tasks despite retaining all feedback, and without quantitative feedback its motion becomes less precise and the agent less reliably recognizes when task has been completed. 2. Related Work Motion for human-scene interaction. Learned HSI methods synthesize interactions in 3D scenes from interaction data, either kinematically [7, 13, 14, 18, 38, 45, 47, 48, 58, 61, 62, 64] or with physics simulation [8, 25, 40, 44, 46, 50, 54, 55, 59]. These methods are effective for the interaction types and object categories represented in their training data, but are less suited to open-ended long-horizon tasks in which an agent must repeatedly adapt motion to the 2 evolving physical state of scene. complementary line of work trains general motion generators without scene, but allows users to specify spatial constraints in addition to text, such as target positions, paths or poses. Examples include OmniControl [53], Kimodo [32], and related controllable motion generators [2, 4, 15, 16, 19, 26, 27, 42, 65]. Recent systems also let language model write such constraints, usually once, for motion generator [6, 23, 66]. Inhabitant builds on this capability without training, but writes the constraints repeatedly and revises them from measurements of the executed motion. Language agents for human-scene interaction. Agents that direct body in scene differ in what the language model writes: plan for trained controllers or expert models [5, 43, 51], such as UniHSI [52] and World2HOSI [20]; atomic skills, such as HumanCLAW [37]; text for text-tomotion model, such as Motion-Agent [49] and InteractAgent [60]; or spatial targets for motion generator [63], such as GPT-Connect [30], BiBo [12] and GEMS [1]. Among them, InteractAgent is closest in spirit because it revises motion after observing rendered outcomes, but the revision is made through text and relies on qualitative visual feedback. Inhabitant instead revises spatial constraints from metric measurements of the execution. Embodied household tasks. Household benchmarks pose long-horizon tasks with movable objects, such as PARTNR [3] and EmbodiedBench [56], which build on earlier simulated household environments [17, 21, 28, 29, 33 35, 39]. Language agents typically solve these tasks in perception-action loop with feedback from the environment [911, 22, 31, 57]. The closest case is FAEA [41], which refines manipulation program over repeated attempts in simulation. However, these systems generally act through skills, primitives or end-effector commands, including for the humanoid avatars of Habitat 3.0. Inhabit keeps the long-horizon household setting but requires every step to be realized by generated whole-body motion. 3. Inhabitant Inhabitant is training-free agent framework with three components. The agent is connected to the other two components by two interfaces, which are the core of the framework: spatial control, through which it specifies the motion for the generator by positions, paths and poses, and quantitative feedback, through which the simulator reports the executed result as measurements. We first state the problem and then describe the components one by one. 3.1. Problem Formulation An interaction sequence is fixed-frame-rate sequence of states Σ = (s0, . . . , sN ), where each state st comprises the poses of the body, all objects and the articulated furniture at frame t. Here, denotes the number of frames. The agent does not act frame by frame but through segments: segment τk = (stk1 , . . . , stk ) is contiguous, few-second portion of the sequence that is generated and executed as unit. The full sequence is the concatenation of segments, Σ = (τ1, . . . , τK). The input is natural-language instruction and the initial state s0. Task completion is evaluated by success rule G, which checks the states of the sequence and returns 1 for success and 0 otherwise. The rule is task-specific, defined together with its instruction (Sec. 4), and hidden from the agent. The objective is to produce successful interaction sequence Σ such that G(Σ) = 1. 3.2. Agent The agent π is language model that builds the interaction sequence segment by segment. The prompt of the agent contains the instruction I, the state description ϕ(s0) of the initial state, the documentation of the generator, the dimensions of the simulated body, and the request for person-like motion that neither collides with the scene nor slides its feet (Supp. A.2). These calls build the interaction sequence in loop; pseudocode is given in the supplement (Algorithm 1). The loop ends when the success rule is satisfied after commit, when the agent stops issuing calls, or when the budget of calls to the language model is used up. The sequence Σ built up to that point is returned. 3.3. Motion Generator: Spatial Control The motion generator provides the spatial control interface to the agent. We adopt Kimodo [32], pretrained generator of whole-body motion conditioned on text and spatial constraints. For each TRY call, Kimodo converts the control specification into motion where is sequence of whole-body poses at the frame rate of the sequence, conditioned on the motion at the end of the preceding segment. The control specification is written by the agent in the input format of Kimodo, which is documented in its prompt. It has three parts. First, timeline of text prompts with their durations, generated one after another. Second, set of spatial constraints K, through which the agent exerts spatial control: each fixes set of specified joints at specified frame to target position or pose. Kimodo supports three types of constraints: root waypoints, which fix the position of the root on the ground and optionally its heading, endeffector targets, which fix hand or foot, and full-body keyframes, which fix all joints. Third, the sampling parameters, namely the random seed and the guidance weights for text and constraints. The agent uses no intermediate representation between the agent and Kimodo. Since full-body keyframe is written as joint rotations, the agent can ask by forward kinematics where the joints of pose would be, for example hand, before it uses the pose in try. The tasks are organized into four tiers (Fig. 3c, e): 30 low tasks with one goal, 20 mid tasks with two goals, 15 high tasks with three goals, and 10 posture tasks that combine goal with posture. Main Results With Claude Opus 5.5, Inhabitant satisfies the success rule on 74 of the 75 tasks, whereas the best baseline using the same language model reaches only 26.7% success (Tab. 2). The gap widens with task length: the baselines solve some low tier tasks but almost none of the midand high-tier tasks. Each baseline fails at the interface it lacks. Since all baselines share the same language model, lacking specific interface causes each to fail with distinct cost patInteractAgent has feedback but no spatial contern. trol: it can observe what went wrong but can only reword It therefore needs three times as many its text prompts. tries as Inhabitant and most failures use up the budget. HumanCLAW is limited to fixed set of skills that cannot place hand precisely enough to interact with an object; the agent recognizes this and stops by itself in every failure, after about dozen calls. GEMS has spatial control but no feedback: the errors of its single plan accumulate, most of its grasps miss, and it succeeds only on tasks with loose targets such as kicking or throwing. Fig. 4 shows these failure modes on one task. The interfaces matter more than the choice of the language model. Across five language models, the success of Inhabitant follows model capability: the three stronger models solve at least 82.7% of the tasks, and the two weaker ones solve less than half, mostly in the low tier and posture tasks. Nevertheless, both weaker models with Inhabitants interfaces outperform every baseline with Claude Opus 5.5. The weaker models gain less from each revision: after missed grasp, revised try of Claude Opus 5.5 succeeds twice as often as one of the weaker models (Supp. D.2). As result, weaker models need more tries, collide more often, and mostly fail by using up the budget. Inhabitant is also cheaper per solved task: $1.7 in API fees with Claude Opus 5.5, against $4.8 to $21.1 for the baselines (Supp. D.1). 5.3. On all 75 tasks without the success check, Inhabitant still achieves 86.7% success, and nine of ten episodes in which it stops by itself are successful (Supp. D.4). Thus, quantitative measurements allow the agent to verify the outcome by itself in most episodes. 5.5. Further Analysis In Inhabitant, the agent may revise try using feedback as many times as needed before committing it (Sec. 3.2). To assess the value of this revision loop, we compare Inhabitant with two settings that remove it (Tab. 5). In SingleTry, each try is committed as soon as it is executed, so the agent still receives feedback but can only correct mistake in later segments (similar to ReAct [57]). In Open-Loop, the agent writes all control specifications at once, and they are executed without any feedback. Open-Loop solves no task, since nothing corrects the deviations of the executed motion from the plan. Single-Try solves four tasks fewer than Inhabitant, and its body collides about four times as often, because every imprecise try stays in the interaction sequence. Revising try before committing it therefore helps success and, more importantly, keeps the interaction sequence clean. The scene simulator moves the body kinematically, without balance or torques. To test whether the interaction sequences are nevertheless physically plausible, we track those of Inhabitant with Claude Opus 5.5 with the pretrained physics controller PHC+ [24] on flat floor, in the parts where the body is not supported by furniture. The controller follows 94% of these parts without falling, and half of its failures are in tasks that end in kneeling or lying posture (Supp. D.6). 6. Conclusion and Future Work We presented Inhabitant, training-free agent framework for long-horizon human-scene interaction that gives the agent what existing agents lack: spatial control over the motion and quantitative feedback on its execution. To evaluate such interaction, we built Inhabit, benchmark of 75 household tasks in which every step is carried out by the motion of the whole body and success rule decides on the physical outcome. On Inhabit, Inhabitant completes 98.7% of the tasks with Claude Opus 5.5, where existing agentic HSI baselines complete at most 26.7% with the same language model, and the ablations confirm that both interfaces are needed: without spatial control the agent fails most tasks, and without quantitative feedback its motion is less precise. Inhabitant has four main limitations. First, it requires scene simulator in which motion can be tried repeatedly, making it best suited for offline uses such as animation and data generation; an online setting, where every executed motion is irreversible, are better reflected by the Single-Try results in Sec. 5.5. Second, the body is driven kinematically, without balance, torques or fingers, and grasping is rule-based; pretrained physics controller already follows 8 most of the interaction sequences (Sec. 5.5), and driving the body with such controller is future work. Third, the agent is given the state description of the scene and success check after each try; it still solves most tasks without the check (Sec. 5.4), and replacing the given state by perception is left for future work. Fourth, because of budget constraints, each task is run once and the ablations use 20-task subset. Moreover, the baselines are our adaptations. Future evaluations should include repeated runs and comparisons with the original implementations.

sections.title: LLM Usage Statement
sections.content: LLMs are an object of study in this work: the agent of Inhabitant is an LLM that is used without training. We evaluate Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Sonnet 5.5, Gemini 4 Argon, gpt-6-luna and the open-weight GLM-5.3-Flash as this agent, and Claude Opus 5.5 as the agent of the adapted baselines (Sec. 5.1). In addition, we used Claude as an assistant for writing and debugging the code of the agent, the benchmark and the evaluation, for launching and monitoring experiment runs and computing the reported statistics, for surveying related work, and for drafting and editing parts of the manuscript text and figures. The research questions, method design, benchmark tasks, experimental protocol and conclusions are the authors own. All LLM-assisted code, text, figures and citations were reviewed and verified by the authors, and all reported results come from our own runs.

The system prompt has two parts. The second part is the public documentation of Kimodo, copied unchanged: its pages on the constraints, on their JSON format (coordinate space and units, constraint types, examples), on the generation parameters and on best practices (text prompting, constraints, limitations), about 11,000 characters. The system prompt is the same for every task and every language model, and it names no object, no piece of furniture and no task. 13 Tab. 6 lists the tools that implement the four calls of Eq. Besides the four calls, the agent can request the state description of the current state at any time. Fig. 7 shows try, measurement and commit of one episode as the agent issues them and as they are answered. Call Tool and arguments Result TRY(c, e) MEASURE(q) success check and eight rendered frames of the try generate segment: text durations, prompts, constraints, seed, postprocessing, guidance weights (c) and interaction events (e) inspect: list of queries one value or time series COMMIT commit ROLLBACK(j) retry from: index of committed segment get state per query state description within 2 of the body state description full state description Table 6. Choice of motion generator We compare Kimodo with OmniControl [53], text-tomotion model with spatial control of joints, and with Kimodo given only text prompts, as plain text-to-motion model. The control specifications are those of the segments that Claude Opus 5.5 committed in the main runs. Over all 526 committed segments, 8.7% contain full-body keyframe, 1.3% several text prompts and 65.8% heading of the root, none of which OmniControl takes as input. In addition, 85.7% of the segments continue from the executed end of the previous one, while OmniControl starts every motion from its own canonical first frame. To compare the generators on what both can express, we sample 120 committed segments without full-body keyframes or several text prompts, 60 with only root waypoints and 60 with end-effector targets. Every control specification is generated once from standing start with the same seed. OmniControl receives the same text prompt and duration, the pelvis position on the ground for each root waypoint, and the 3D positions of the constrained joints for each endSystem prompt (part 1 of 2) # Moving with Kimodo You move by asking motion generator, Kimodo, for one segment of motion at time. Its own documentation is at the end ("Kimodos documentation"). generate_segment takes Kimodos inputs: - text: description of the motion, or list of descriptions that are generated one after another; - seconds: its length (one per text); segment is 0.5 to 8 s, each text at most 10 s; - constraints: Kimodos constraint list (its JSON format), in Kimodos frame of this segment; - seed (default 0; the same inputs with the same seed give the same motion; its execution in the simulator can still differ by few cm between identical tries), post (post-processing, default true), cfg_weight ([text, constraint], default [2, 2]). Kimodos frame of segment: the origin is on the floor below your pelvis at the start of the segment, +Z is the direction you face at the start, is up, is to your left; frame_indices count frames from the start of the segment, 30 per second. The other tools report positions as forward / left of your pelvis and heights above the floor: Kimodos / / Y. The skeleton has 22 joints, in this order (one rotation each in local_joints_rot): pelvis, left_hip, right_hip, spine1, left_knee, right_knee, spine2, left_ankle, right_ankle, spine3, left_foot, right_foot, neck, left_collar, right_collar, head, left_shoulder, right_shoulder, left_elbow, right_elbow, left_wrist, right_wrist. local_joints_rot are SMPL-Xs local joint rotations: with all of them zero the body stands in T-pose facing +Z, arms along X. global_root_heading [cos theta, sin theta] is the facing as its (Z, X) components: theta = 0 faces +Z, theta = 90 deg faces +X (turned to the left). hand constraint fixes the wrist (position and rotation), foot constraint the ankle and the toe joint; both also fix the roots position, height and facing at that frame. Every segment starts from your actual pose: Kimodo gets the last frames of what your body did as full-body keyframe just before the segment. The generated motion is fitted to your body, placed in the scene and executed in physics simulator. ## Your task You are the mind of person in an apartment, and you must complete household task by moving your own body. Nothing happens by itself: every movement is segment of motion that you have Kimodo make (above). You act only through the tools. Move as real person would: do not bump into furniture, walls, plants or other things (only your hands touch what you grasp or hold), and do not let your feet slide on the floor. ### Tools - generate_segment(intent, text, seconds, constraints, seed, post, cfg_weight, events): Kimodo makes one segment from the last committed state, executed in physics simulator (furniture and walls stop the body). It returns whether the goal is now satisfied and video of the try (left: camera following you; right: side camera looking at you and at the target of the segment); measure anything else with inspect. Nothing is kept until you commit: every try starts again from the last committed state. - commit(): keeps the last try; the world continues from where it ended. Returns the new state near you (within 2 m; get_state() gives all of it). - get_state(): the current state. - retry_from(i): undo: puts the world back to the start of committed segment and drops segments i..end; then try / commit as before. - inspect(queries): read-only measurements of the world and of your tries: where things and body parts are (now or over try), distances over time, body contacts, the size of any thing, an executed pose in Kimodos format and the joint positions of pose in Kimodos format. It changes nothing. The episode ends when segment you commit completes the task. After each try, look at the result and the video and change the inputs until the segment does what you intended; then commit it. Figure 5. We measure the errors at the constrained frames in the frame of the segment, after resampling OmniControl from 20 to 30 frames per second. Kimodo reaches the end-effector targets almost exactly and the root waypoints within few centimetres (Tab. 8). OmniControl reaches the median root waypoint within 2 cm, but one in ten misses by more than 25 cm, and 81% of its end-effector targets are within 10 cm. It cannot set the heading, which the agent uses in two thirds of its segments to face an object or piece of furniture. It also takes about 25 times as long per segment, which would add about half an hour of generation to an episode of 18 tries. Text prompts 14 alone miss the targets by metres, as with InteractAgent in the main paper. Foot skate of the generated motion is higher for Kimodo (19.7% of frames, 27.7% in segments with only root waypoints) than for OmniControl (13.0%) and for text prompts only (13.6%), so we do not claim better motion quality for Kimodo. The comparison has limits. Tracking the motions with physics controller (Sec. 5.5) Half-physics has no balance model (Sec. 4), so we test whether physically simulated humanoid with balance and torques can follow the interaction sequences. We track the interaction sequence of each of the 75 episodes of Claude Opus 5.5 with the pretrained PHC+ controller [24] in Isaac Gym, on flat floor without furniture or objects. Parts where the body is supported by furniture cannot be tracked without the furniture, so we remove every interval in which body part other than the feet touches furniture for at least 0.3 or foot stands on it, with 0.5 on each side, and track each remaining window of at least 1.5 separately, starting from the pose and velocity of its first frame. This gives 171 windows covering 73% of the frames. We leave out the first 0.5 of each window and count window as failed when the mean joint error exceeds 0.5 m, the criterion of PHC.
